name: Back extension / deadlift strength

lead: Deadlifts and back extensions train the muscles along the back of the body: the spinal erectors, glutes, hamstrings, traps and lats. People use them to stand and sit more upright and to build a thicker, wider-looking back that reads as a broader, taller frame.

The deadlift lifts a weight from the floor to hip level and is one of the three powerlifting lifts. The back extension arches the spine back from a bent-forward position, bodyweight or loaded. The chain is stronger back and hip muscles, easier upright carriage, then a fuller frame. Both are standard strength exercises; no trial has tested them for posture appearance specifically.

paras: Deadlifts are done with a barbell or trap bar as part of a regular lifting routine, usually alongside rows and pulling work. Back extensions are done on a Roman chair, 45-degree bench or reverse-hyperextension machine, or with no equipment, often as a lighter accessory movement. Beginners typically start light and build load over weeks and months, with muscle and posture changes showing gradually as strength rises.

Rounding the back under heavy load is a common form error, described as controversial and a possible factor in injury. Trap-bar deadlifts are described as generally less taxing on the lower back, and back extension guidance advises lighter loads for beginners. Anyone with existing back problems may want to check with a clinician or coach first.

angle.text: Deadlifts and back extensions build the spinal erectors, glutes and upper back, which helps you stand and sit more upright and gives a fuller, wider-looking back. The path runs from a stronger posterior chain to easier upright carriage to a broader, taller-looking frame. They are standard strength training; posture appearance specifically has not been trialled.

lead: Deadlifts and back extensions are posterior-chain exercises that build the muscles running down the back of the body: the glutes, hamstrings and the erector spinae along the spine, with the lats and traps also working in the deadlift.[1][2] Lifters use them to develop a thicker, more muscular back and hips, a fuller glute and hamstring line, and a trunk that holds an upright posture, which together change how the physique reads from behind and from the side.

The deadlift lifts a weight from the floor to hip level and lowers it again, most often with a barbell; it is one of the three powerlifting lifts and a strongman event.[1][3] The back extension, also called hyperextension, strengthens the erector spinae by arching the spine back from a bent-forward position on a Roman chair, a 45-degree bench or a reverse-hyperextension machine, or with no equipment.[2] Variants such as the Romanian deadlift, stiff-leg deadlift, trap-bar deadlift and rack pull shift the emphasis between hips, hamstrings, back and quadriceps.[1][4]

Research on these lifts is largely biomechanical: electromyography reviews of which muscles each variant activates, injury surveys of powerlifters, endurance tests for the back extensors, and trials comparing glute exercises for muscle growth.[5][6][6][6][6] Posture itself is linked in psychology research to how confident and open a person looks to others, and the erector spinae are described as working with the glutes to maintain stable posture standing or sitting.[7][8]

paras: The posterior chain is the group of muscles on the back of the body that extend the hips and spine. The erector spinae form three columns on each side of the spine, the iliocostalis, longissimus and spinalis, running from the sacrum and hips to the base of the skull, and their job is to extend the vertebral column.[8] Wikipedia notes that the erector spinae work with the gluteus maximus, medius and minimus to maintain stable posture standing or sitting.[8]

Deadlifts load these muscles heavily and together, and back extensions isolate the spinal erectors with a lighter load and a longer set. Programmes shared on training forums frequently combine the two, along with good mornings and rows, for back and hip development.[9][10]

The conventional deadlift is described as working the gluteus maximus most, with the quadriceps, hamstrings, trapezius, latissimus dorsi and erector spinae also involved; during setup the glutes, traps and hamstrings load eccentrically while the lumbar muscles contract isometrically to stabilise the spine.[1][4] Wikipedia divides the lift into setup, drive (the most demanding phase) and lockout, in which the lifter stands fully upright with hips extended and glutes and abdominals squeezed.[1][4] In raw powerlifting, grip strength is described as a deciding factor, and the lift is performed with a double overhand, mixed or hook grip.[1]
For looks, the appeal is that one lift loads most of the back of the body at once, which proponents link to back thickness, glute and hamstring development and a stronger-looking trunk.

Variations include the sumo stance, rack pulls (which start higher and allow heavier loads), deficit, paused, single-leg, trap-bar (hex-bar) and stiff-leg deadlifts.[1] The trap bar uses side handles and is described as generally less taxing on the lower back.[1][4] The Romanian deadlift (RDL) starts from standing with the bar already raised, a slight knee bend and a hip hinge with a flat back; it was popularised by Romanian weightlifters, and one of them, Nicu Vlad, coined the name.[4] The stiff-leg version uses minimal knee bend with the torso kept roughly parallel to the floor, and the B-stance RDL puts most of the load on the front leg.[4]

The deadlift entered the standard powerlifting set in the 1960s: in Britain it replaced the biceps curl in the "Strength Set" in 1966 to match American lifts, and the International Powerlifting Federation was formed in 1972, with its first world championships in 1973.[3] Powerlifting allows both conventional and sumo stances, while strongman permits only conventional; straps are banned in powerlifting but allowed in most strongman events.[1][3] Wikipedia also lists record pulls above 500 kilograms in equipped and strongman settings, including Hafthor Julius Bjornsson's 501 kg equipped lift in 2020.[1]

The back extension works the erector spinae. In the 90-degree Roman chair version the body lies horizontally for full range of motion, while the 45-degree bench gives a shorter range, and holding a weight to the chest adds resistance. The reverse hyperextension machine is described as also working the glutes and part of the hamstrings, and a 2019 biomechanical study in the Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research by Lawrence, Chin and Swanson reportedly compared it with the standard hyperextension and found relatively more hip range of motion.[2] The no-equipment version has the lifter lying prone and raising arms, torso and legs, so that gravity provides the resistance.[2]
Wikipedia points out that anatomically the spinal movement is flexion-extension rather than true hyperextension, and distinguishes the exercise from joint hypermobility or a hyperextension injury.[2]

Back-extensor strength is measured in research with isometric endurance tests such as the Sorensen test, and a literature review found six types of such tests, with the motivation and effort of the subject as limiting factors.[5] A study of lumbar back-extensor mechanics examined how torque is produced about the lumbar spine.[11]

sections.h: Related lifts for the back of the body
paras: Good mornings, reverse hypers, Romanian deadlifts, stiff-leg deadlifts, hip thrusts and rows are the exercises that most often appear next to the deadlift and back extension in programmes.[9][10] Members of the T Nation forum list stiff-legged and Romanian deadlifts, hip thrusts and back extensions among their staples, and one posted four-week programme pairs a deadlift day with good mornings, weighted back extensions and Pendlay rows.[9][10]

A 2020 PLoS One systematic review by Martin-Fuentes and colleagues covered surface electromyography studies of deadlift variants in healthy, trained adults. It found the biceps femoris the most studied muscle, followed by the gluteus maximus, vastus lateralis and erector spinae, and reported higher activation in the erector spinae and quadriceps than in the gluteus maximus and biceps femoris. The Romanian deadlift produced lower erector spinae activation than biceps femoris and semitendinosus activation. The authors called for standardised methods.[6]

A 2022 study of ten competitive bodybuilders measured six posterior-chain muscles at 80% of one-repetition maximum in the Romanian, step-Romanian and stiff-leg deadlift. In the ascending phase the step-Romanian produced greater activation than the other two in several muscles, including the gluteus maximus, semitendinosus and longissimus; the authors linked this to its greater range of motion and stretch.[6]

For glute size, a 9-week trial of 34 untrained adults compared volume-matched hip thrust and back squat training and found similar gluteal muscle growth, with differences leaning slightly toward the hip thrust; the squat group gained more thigh muscle, and deadlift strength rose similarly in both groups.[6] A 2018 narrative review of powerlifting injuries notes that pain and injuries are common among lifters, with possible causes including heavy loads, large ranges of motion, insufficient rest between sessions and faulty technique.[6]

Posture-minded lifters expect a stronger back and glutes to make standing and sitting tall easier, which changes silhouette and presence. Psychology research cited on Wikipedia reports that open postures are often perceived as friendly and positive, that a confident posture changed how participants in a 2009 study rated themselves, and that a hunched posture was associated with reported stress in a 1982 study; the article also advises reading posture in context.[7] No trial has tested deadlifts or back extensions as a way to change posture or perceived confidence, so the link remains an inference from muscle function.[7][8]

Common deadlift errors listed include protracting the shoulders, letting the bar drift from the body, rounding the back and turning the lift into a squat. The article says whether back rounding is harmful is controversial and that excessive rounding may lead to injury, and describes the trap-bar variant as generally less taxing on the lower back.[1] For back extensions, the only explicit guidance in the encyclopedia article is that beginners can use lighter weights to avoid straining the back muscles.[2] Belts are allowed in both powerlifting and strongman, and equipped lifters may use deadlift suits.[1][3]

On the T Nation forum, back extensions, good mornings, reverse hypers and deadlifts appear together in posted programmes aimed at the lower back and posterior chain, and members list stiff-legged deadlifts, Romanian deadlifts, hip thrusts and back extensions among their staple lifts.[9][10]

No studies found testing deadlifts or back extensions as an intervention for appearance or posture. Related research includes the electromyography reviews and the hip-thrust trial above, a review of isometric back-extension endurance tests, a randomised comparison of integrated versus isolated core exercises using muscle activation in the erector spinae, rectus abdominis and obliques, and a systematic review of physical functioning measures as predictors in low back pain.[5][12][13][6][6]

lore.intro: In strength and looksmaxxing circles, deadlifts and back extensions are discussed as the core of posterior-chain training, mentioned alongside rows, good mornings and hip thrusts in programmes shared on T Nation.[9][10]
